verifyNote: Written from the joint professional duty of candour statement, GOC guidance and UK law. Always check against Dr Bartlett's session and the current GOC guidance on optical.org.

topics.title: What the professional duty of candour requires
topics.summary: Every healthcare professional must be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong with their care that causes, or could cause, harm or distress. The UK healthcare regulators (including the GOC) set this out together in a joint statement on the professional duty of candour.
keyPoints: Tell the patient (or their carer/advocate) when something has gone wrong.
Apologise.
Offer an appropriate remedy or support to put matters right if possible.
Explain fully the short- and long-term effects of what has happened.
Be open and honest with colleagues, employers and regulators; take part in reviews and investigations.
Report adverse incidents and near misses through the right systems so lessons are learned.
The professional duty applies to individuals; there's also a separate statutory duty of candour for organisations (e.g. Regulation 20 in England, overseen by the CQC).
examTraps: Thinking candour only applies when actual harm occurs — it includes potential harm and distress.
Mixing up the professional (individual) duty with the statutory (organisational) duty.
Believing an apology admits legal liability.

diagram.description: Four steps in a row with arrows: Tell → Apologise → Put right / support → Explain effects. Below: 'Report and learn' feeding back into practice.

goDeeper.heading: Examples in optometry
goDeeper.body: Wrong prescription dispensed; lenses glazed with the wrong axis; a missed or delayed referral; a corneal abrasion from contact tonometry; an allergic reaction to drops; records sent to the wrong patient. Each needs honesty with the patient, an apology, practical steps to put it right and reporting.

goDeeper.heading: As a student
goDeeper.body: If something goes wrong in clinic, tell your supervisor straight away — don't try to hide or fix it alone. The supervisor will help with talking to the patient and recording it. Being candid as a student is part of the GOC Standards for Optical Students.

flashcards.front: Four things the duty of candour requires with patients
flashcards.back: Tell, apologise, offer remedy/support, explain effects.
Professional = individuals (regulators); statutory = organisations (e.g. CQC Regulation 20 in England).

flashcards.front: Does candour apply to potential harm?
flashcards.back: Yes — harm or potential harm and distress.

mcq.q: You realise you gave a patient the wrong axis on their prescription last week. What does candour require?

options.text: Contact them, apologise, put it right and report it
options.feedback: Yes — that's the duty in full.

options.text: Wait to see whether the patient notices
Quietly correct the axis on the record
options.feedback: Altering records to hide errors is serious misconduct.

options.text: Only tell the patient if they complain

mcq.explanation: Be open, apologise, fix it (e.g. remake the glasses), explain any effects and report through the right system.

mcq.q: What does the professional duty of candour require first?

options.text: Telling the patient something went wrong
Hiding the error to avoid worry

mcq.explanation: Candour starts with openness: the patient must be told that something has gone wrong, not kept in the dark or told only via others.

mcq.q: Which is part of the duty?
mcq.explanation: The duty includes a sincere apology. Saying sorry isn't the same as admitting legal liability, and compensation isn't automatically required.

mcq.q: You discover a colleague's mistake was entered on the wrong patient's record. Besides the patient, who must you be honest with?

options.text: Colleagues, employer and, if needed, the regulator
Nobody else: candour is only owed to patients
Your friends, who can give you advice
The patient's family, instead of the patient

mcq.explanation: Be open and honest with colleagues, employers and regulators, and take part in reviews.

original.q: Who else must you be honest with?

mcq.q: Why report near misses?

options.text: So lessons are learned and harm prevented
So that someone can be blamed for it
It's optional and rarely helps anyone
So that staff can earn a reward for it

mcq.explanation: Near misses show where a system could fail. Reporting them lets the team learn and fix the problem before someone is harmed.

mcq.q: What should you explain to the patient?

options.text: Only what it will cost to fix
Only the good news about it

mcq.explanation: Patients need to know the likely short- and long-term effects of what happened, so they can make informed decisions about their care.

mcq.q: Which statement about the duty of candour is wrong?

options.text: The statutory duty applies to individual students
options.feedback: Yes, that's wrong: it applies to organisations.

options.text: The professional duty applies to individual registrants
Both require openness when things go wrong

mcq.explanation: The professional duty applies to individuals; the statutory duty applies to organisations.

original.q: The statutory duty of candour applies to

options.feedback: Yes; the professional duty applies to individuals.

mcq.q: A patient's new glasses had the wrong axis. Besides telling and apologising, what should you offer?

options.text: A remedy, such as remaking the glasses, and support
A discount on their next frame only

mcq.explanation: Offer an appropriate remedy or support to put matters right if possible.

original.q: What should you offer if possible?

options.text: A remedy or support to put things right

mcq.q: Do students have a duty of candour?

options.feedback: Yes: the student standards include being candid.

mcq.explanation: The GOC's standards for optical students include being candid when things go wrong, so the duty applies to students too.

mcq.q: Should you take part in investigations?
mcq.explanation: Being candid includes co-operating openly and honestly with investigations, so the cause can be found and fixed.

mcq.q: Which statement is wrong?

options.text: The 2014 statement came only from the NHS
options.feedback: Yes, that's wrong: it came from the healthcare regulators, including the GOC.

options.text: The GOC was one of its signatories
It applies to optometrists in practice
It sets out a professional duty of candour

mcq.explanation: The joint statement on the professional duty of candour (2014) was issued by the healthcare regulators, including the GOC.

original.q: Who issued the joint statement on the professional duty of candour (2014)?

options.text: The healthcare regulators, including the GOC

mcq.q: When should the patient be told something has gone wrong?
mcq.explanation: Patients should be told promptly, as soon as reasonably practicable, so they can get any care they need and trust isn't damaged.

mcq.q: The statutory duty of candour uses the term
mcq.explanation: The statutory duty of candour (for organisations) is triggered by a 'notifiable safety incident': an unexpected incident causing moderate or severe harm, or death.

mcq.q: A student who notices an error should
mcq.explanation: Students work under supervision, so they should tell their supervisor straight away; the supervisor can then make sure the patient is told and the error put right.

mcq.q: What should be recorded?

options.text: What happened and what the patient was told
Only who was to blame for it
A cover story agreed by the team

mcq.explanation: The record should show what happened and what the patient was told, so the conversation and any follow-up can be checked later.

mcq.q: Why does candour matter for learning?

options.text: It helps the team stop repeats
So the team can punish errors

mcq.explanation: When errors are shared openly, the team can see what went wrong and change systems so it doesn't happen again.

mcq.q: Should you stop a colleague raising a concern?
mcq.explanation: You must never try to stop someone raising a concern; doing so puts patients at risk and breaches the GOC standards.

mcq.q: A 'culture of openness' means

options.text: staff feel safe to report errors
staff hide errors to protect the team
staff are blamed for every error

mcq.explanation: An open culture is one where staff feel safe to report errors and concerns without fear of unfair blame.

mcq.q: Candour applies when something goes wrong that

options.text: has caused or could cause harm

mcq.explanation: Candour applies when something has caused, or could cause, harm or distress. Near misses with no effect should still be reported for learning.

mcq.q: What should be offered to put things right?

options.text: A remedy or support, where possible
A discount on the next purchase

mcq.explanation: Candour means offering an appropriate remedy or support to put things right where possible, as well as an apology and explanation.

mcq.q: Who does the professional duty of candour apply to?
mcq.explanation: The professional duty of candour applies to every individual GOC registrant, including students; the statutory duty applies to organisations.

mcq.q: Who does the statutory duty of candour mainly apply to?

options.text: Organisations registered with the CQC or similar
Patients who make a formal complaint
Nobody: it isn't written into any law

mcq.explanation: The statutory duty of candour is a legal requirement on organisations registered with the CQC (and equivalents elsewhere), rather than on individuals.

mcq.q: A patient was given the wrong drops but noticed nothing. What does candour require?

options.text: Tell them, apologise and check for effects
Say nothing, as there was no harm
Hide the bottle and replace it
Blame the patient for not noticing

mcq.explanation: Even if the patient noticed nothing, the error must be disclosed: tell them, apologise and check whether the drops had any effect.

mcq.q: A wrong drop was picked up but caught before instilling. What should you do?

options.text: Report it as a near miss
Nothing, as no harm was done
Tell only your friends about it
Throw away the record of it

mcq.explanation: An error caught before it reaches the patient is a near miss. Reporting it helps the team find and fix the weak point.

mcq.q: A referral letter was never sent and the patient's appointment is delayed. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them, apologise, send it urgently and report it
Send the letter quietly and say nothing
Blame the post for losing the letter
Ignore it, as the appointment will come

mcq.explanation: The patient has been affected by the delay, so candour means telling them, apologising, sending the referral urgently and reporting the incident.

mcq.q: A letter with one patient's details was posted to another patient. What's this?

options.text: A data breach to be open about and report
Nothing, as it was an honest mistake
A joke that the team can laugh about
A near miss, as no harm was done

mcq.explanation: Sending one patient's details to another is a personal data breach. It must be reported (possibly to the ICO) and the affected patient told.

mcq.q: A patient trips over a box in the practice and bruises their arm. What's needed?

options.text: Help them, record it, apologise and report it
Ignore it, as it was only a bruise
Ask them to sign a waiver form

mcq.explanation: The patient was harmed on the premises, so they need help first, then the incident should be recorded, apologised for and reported.

mcq.q: A spectacle Rx was dispensed with the wrong PD and caused headaches. Candour means

options.text: telling them to keep wearing them to adapt
charging them for the remake as usual
saying nothing and remaking them quietly

mcq.explanation: The headaches came from a dispensing error, so the patient should be told what went wrong, given an apology and have the glasses remade at no cost.

mcq.q: A 'just culture' means

options.text: errors can be reported safely, with fair accountability
nobody is ever held accountable for anything
everyone is blamed whenever something goes wrong
errors are kept quiet to protect the team

mcq.explanation: A just culture makes it safe to report errors while still holding people fairly to account for reckless or deliberate acts.

mcq.q: Why should honesty extend to regulators and employers?

options.text: They need the facts to protect patients
So that you stay out of trouble
It doesn't need to extend to them
Only if they ask you directly

mcq.explanation: Regulators and employers can only protect patients if they have the facts, so you must be honest with them too, not only when asked.

mcq.q: What should you avoid when explaining an error?

options.text: Guessing or blaming before the facts are known

mcq.explanation: Speculating or blaming before the facts are known can mislead the patient and be unfair to colleagues. Stick to what is known.

mcq.q: Under the statutory duty, a notifiable safety incident involves

options.text: unexpected moderate or severe harm, or death
any minor delay to an appointment
an incident where no harm occurred
a near miss caught before it happened

mcq.explanation: A notifiable safety incident involves unexpected harm that is moderate or severe, or death. Near misses and no-harm incidents aren't notifiable, though still reported.

mcq.q: The statutory duty requires the organisation to follow up with
mcq.explanation: Under the statutory duty, the organisation must follow the conversation with a written account and an apology.

mcq.q: Why does candour build trust?

options.text: Patients feel respected by the truth
It doesn't build trust at all

mcq.explanation: Patients trust clinicians who tell them the truth, even when it's difficult. Hiding errors damages that trust when they come out.

mcq.q: A colleague asks you to keep quiet about their error. What should you do?

options.text: Encourage openness, and raise it yourself if needed
Keep quiet, out of loyalty to your colleague
Post about it anonymously on social media
Help them quietly change the record

mcq.explanation: Patient safety comes before loyalty. Encourage the colleague to be open, and if they won't, raise the concern yourself.

mcq.q: Expired drops were used on a patient. What should happen?

options.text: Tell the patient, assess risk and report it
Nothing, as the effect is probably minor
Blame the supplier for the dates

mcq.explanation: Using expired drops is an error that could affect the patient, so tell them, assess any risk and report it.

mcq.q: When something goes wrong, who should usually speak to the patient?

options.text: A suitable professional involved in their care
The receptionist, as the first contact
The patient's family, instead of them

mcq.explanation: The conversation should be led by a suitable professional involved in the patient's care, who can explain what happened and what happens next.

mcq.q: Candour includes telling the patient about
mcq.explanation: Candour includes explaining the likely short- and long-term effects, so the patient knows what to expect and can make choices.

mcq.q: A student realises they recorded the wrong eye's IOP. What should they do?

options.text: Tell the supervisor and correct it properly
Delete the wrong entry from the record
Ignore it, as the values are close

mcq.explanation: The supervisor needs to know, and the record must be corrected properly: a dated, signed amendment, never deleting or hiding the original.

mcq.q: Why record what you said to the patient after an error?

options.text: It shows openness and helps investigations
To protect yourself and nothing more
It's not needed if you apologised
So the practice can bill for the time

mcq.explanation: A record of what was said shows you were open, and helps any later investigation or review understand what happened.

mcq.q: Which GOC standard theme covers this duty?

options.text: Being candid when things go wrong

mcq.explanation: GOC standard 'Be candid when things have gone wrong' sets out the professional duty of candour.

mcq.q: Should fear of a complaint stop you being open?
mcq.explanation: Fear of a complaint must never stop you being open; candour is a professional duty whatever the consequences.

mcq.q: A patient asks directly if a mistake was made. What should you do?

options.text: Answer honestly with what you know
Refuse to discuss it at all

mcq.explanation: If a patient asks directly, you must answer honestly with what you know, explaining that more will be shared once it's investigated.

mcq.q: Organisations should support staff after incidents because

options.text: staff can be distressed and need help to learn

mcq.explanation: Staff involved in incidents can be distressed. Supporting them helps them recover and learn, and keeps the culture open.

mcq.q: Being candid also means telling colleagues when

options.text: you spot a risk to patients

mcq.explanation: Candour isn't only about errors after the event: if you spot a risk to patients, you should tell colleagues so it can be dealt with.

mcq.q: What's the risk of a culture where errors are hidden?
mcq.explanation: If errors are hidden, nobody learns from them, so the same mistakes keep happening and more patients are harmed.

mcq.q: A dispensing error is found before the patient collects. What should you do?

options.text: Correct it and log a near miss
Blame the lab and move on

mcq.explanation: An error caught before it reached the patient is a near miss: correct it, then log it so the cause can be addressed.

mcq.q: How soon should a patient be told about a harmful incident?
mcq.explanation: Patients should be told as soon as reasonably practicable; delaying for blame or legal advice isn't acceptable.

mcq.q: Candour applies even when

options.text: the patient doesn't know anything went wrong
the patient already knows about the error
nothing at all has actually happened
the error happened at the weekend

mcq.explanation: Candour applies even when the patient is unaware anything went wrong; you must tell them, not wait to be found out.

mcq.q: Why should you offer further investigation or treatment after an error?

options.text: To put things right where possible
It isn't needed after an apology

mcq.explanation: Candour includes offering any further investigation or treatment needed to put things right for the patient.

cases.scenario: A patient was given spectacles made to another patient's prescription after a labelling mix-up. They wore them for two weeks and had headaches before the error was found.
cases.question: What does the duty of candour require you to do?
cases.modelAnswer: Tell the patient promptly and openly what happened; apologise; explain fully the short and long-term effects (here headaches and blur, with no lasting harm expected); and offer an appropriate remedy and support, such as correct spectacles made urgently at no cost. Record the conversation and what was done. Report the incident through the practice's system so the cause can be found and fixed, and tell the other patient if their information was disclosed. The professional duty applies to you as an individual registrant, whatever your employer does.

topics.askClaude: Explain the professional duty of candour simply, then give me 3 clinic mistakes and ask me exactly what I'd say and do.

topics.title: Apologising and explaining when things go wrong
topics.summary: A good apology is prompt, sincere and specific, and comes with a clear explanation and a plan. Saying sorry is not an admission of legal liability. Patients mostly want to know what happened, that someone cares, and that it won't happen again.
keyPoints: Apologise as soon as practical, ideally face to face, in a private space.
Be specific: 'I'm sorry that your glasses were made with the wrong prescription.'
Explain what happened in plain language, without jargon or blame.
Say what you'll do now and what support is available.
Listen and answer questions; give a point of contact.
In England and Wales, an apology doesn't of itself amount to an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006, s.2).
Record the conversation and follow up as promised.
examTraps: A non-apology ('I'm sorry you feel that way').
Blaming colleagues or the lab in front of the patient.

diagram.description: Speech bubble template split into parts: 'I'm sorry that…' (specific) → 'What happened was…' (explanation) → 'What we'll do now is…' (remedy) → 'If you have any questions…' (support and contact).

goDeeper.heading: An example conversation
goDeeper.body: 'Mrs Ahmed, thank you for coming back in. I'm sorry — your new glasses were made with the wrong strength in the right lens, which is why things looked blurry. That was our error. We'll remake them as a priority at no cost, and I'll check them myself before you collect. In the meantime your old glasses are safe to use. Do you have any questions? Here's my direct number if anything else worries you.'

goDeeper.heading: After the conversation
goDeeper.body: Record what happened, what you said and agreed, and report the incident through your practice's system. Reflect on it (what caused it, what will prevent it) — it's also good material for CPD reflection once you're qualified.

flashcards.back: Prompt, sincere, specific, with explanation and a plan.
Record it, report the incident, follow up, reflect.

mcq.q: Which is the best opening line?

options.text: 'I'm sorry, your glasses were made wrongly: our mistake.'
'The lab must have messed up the order.'
options.feedback: Blames others and isn't an apology.

mcq.explanation: Good apologies name the problem and own it, without blame.

mcq.q: A patient's referral was delayed by a week. When and how should you apologise?

options.text: As soon as practical, ideally face to face in private
After the investigation finishes months later

mcq.explanation: Apologise as soon as practical, ideally face to face, in a private space.

original.q: When should you apologise?

options.text: As soon as practical, ideally face to face in private

mcq.q: Which apology is best?

options.text: 'I'm sorry your glasses were made wrongly'
'Sorry if you feel upset about it'

mcq.explanation: A good apology names what went wrong and takes responsibility. 'I'm sorry if…' or 'sorry you feel…' sounds like dodging.

original.q: Which is a good, specific apology?

options.text: 'I'm sorry your glasses were made with the wrong prescription'

mcq.q: A colleague won't apologise because 'it'll count as admitting negligence'. In England and Wales, is that right?

options.text: No: an apology isn't itself an admission
Yes, an apology always admits negligence
Only if the apology is put in writing
Only if the apology comes from a student

mcq.explanation: In England and Wales, an apology doesn't of itself admit negligence (Compensation Act 2006).

original.q: In England and Wales, does an apology admit negligence?

mcq.q: What should follow the apology?

options.text: What happens now and what support there is
Silence, to let the patient take it in
Changing the subject to the next test
Explaining who was to blame for it

mcq.explanation: After saying sorry, the patient needs to know what happens next and what support is available, so they aren't left uncertain.

mcq.q: At the end of an apology conversation, the patient asks who to call with questions. What should you give them?
mcq.explanation: A named contact gives the patient a clear route for questions and shows you're following it through.

original.q: What should you give the patient?

options.text: A form to sign away rights

mcq.q: Which explanation is best when telling a patient about an error?

options.text: 'The lab set the lens at the wrong angle, so things looked tilted'
'There was an axis transposition error in the minus cylinder'
'The lab messed up your lenses, it wasn't my mistake'
'It's complicated, but we'll make you a new pair'

mcq.explanation: Explain what happened in plain language, without jargon or blame.

original.q: What language should you use?

options.text: Plain language without jargon or blame

mcq.q: What should be recorded?
mcq.explanation: The conversation and the actions agreed should be recorded, so there's a clear account and follow-up isn't missed.

mcq.q: You promised a patient you'd call after checking with the lab. What's the most important thing now?

options.text: Ask a receptionist to say nothing

mcq.explanation: Keeping a promise rebuilds trust, so follow up when you said you would and record that you did.

original.q: What should you do after the conversation?

mcq.q: Why listen and answer questions?

options.text: It helps them understand and rebuilds trust
It wastes time in a busy clinic
It isn't needed after an apology

mcq.explanation: Listening and answering questions helps the patient understand what happened and helps rebuild their trust.

mcq.q: Which response to an upset patient is a poor apology?

options.text: 'I'm sorry we gave the wrong prescription'
'I apologise for the delay in your referral'

mcq.explanation: Avoid conditional or deflecting apologies.

original.q: Which is a poor apology?

options.text: 'I'm sorry we gave the wrong axis'

mcq.q: Where's the best place to apologise?
mcq.explanation: A private, face-to-face conversation is the most respectful way to apologise and lets the patient ask questions.

mcq.q: Who should apologise?

options.text: The right team member, often the one involved
Nobody: a letter from the practice is enough
The receptionist, every time, as first contact
The patient, for having made the complaint

mcq.explanation: The apology should come from the right person, often the clinician involved or a senior colleague, who can explain what happened.

mcq.q: After apologising in person, what should follow?
mcq.explanation: A written follow-up confirms what was discussed and what will happen next, which the patient can refer back to.

mcq.q: Should you blame colleagues when apologising?
mcq.explanation: Blaming colleagues is unprofessional and often premature; the apology is on behalf of the team, and facts come from the investigation.

mcq.q: What should you explain?

options.text: What happened, what it means and what's next

mcq.explanation: A good apology explains what happened, what it means for the patient and what happens next.

mcq.q: Does an apology have to wait until an investigation is finished?

options.text: No: apologise now, share findings later
Yes, always wait for the findings
Only if the patient makes a complaint
Only with a lawyer in the room

mcq.explanation: Don't wait: apologise and explain what's known now, then share the investigation's findings later.

mcq.q: Why use plain language?
mcq.explanation: Plain language makes sure the patient actually understands what happened and what it means for them.

mcq.q: What support might you offer?
mcq.explanation: Offering practical support, such as a further appointment or referral, shows you're trying to put things right.

mcq.q: Which describes a good apology?

options.text: Sincere and specific, followed by what will happen next
Delivered only by letter months later

mcq.explanation: An apology should be sincere and specific, with an explanation and next steps.

original.q: An apology should be

mcq.q: In Scotland, apologies are protected from being used as admissions of liability by
mcq.explanation: The Apologies (Scotland) Act 2016 stops an apology being used as an admission of liability in Scotland. In England and Wales, the Compensation Act 2006 does similar.

mcq.q: Which are elements of a good apology?

options.text: Acknowledge, explain, regret, and next steps
Deny it, then move on quickly to the test
Blame someone else, then leave the room
Stay silent and let the patient do the talking

mcq.explanation: A good apology acknowledges what happened, explains it, expresses genuine regret and sets out the next steps.

mcq.q: Which phrase sounds defensive?
mcq.explanation: 'It's not my fault' deflects responsibility and dismisses the patient's experience, so it sounds defensive.

mcq.q: Who can the patient bring to the conversation?

options.text: A relative or friend, if they wish
Nobody: it must be one to one

mcq.explanation: Patients can bring a relative or friend for support if they want to; it can help them take in what's said.

mcq.q: Why give the patient a named contact?

options.text: So they know who to ask next
It isn't needed after an apology
To stop them phoning the practice

mcq.explanation: A named contact means the patient knows exactly who to go to with further questions, which builds trust.

mcq.q: Where can patients take unresolved optical consumer complaints?
mcq.explanation: The Optical Consumer Complaints Service (OCCS) is the free mediation service for unresolved complaints about optical goods and services.

mcq.q: Unresolved NHS complaints in England can go to
mcq.explanation: If an NHS complaint can't be resolved locally in England, the patient can take it to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman.

mcq.q: Should an apology be scripted word for word?
mcq.explanation: A scripted apology sounds insincere; the key elements should be there, but in your own genuine words.

mcq.q: What should you do if the patient becomes upset during the apology?

options.text: Leave the room until they calm down
Argue that it wasn't so bad

mcq.explanation: If the patient gets upset, pause, listen and acknowledge their feelings before going on.

mcq.q: Why avoid speculation in an apology?

options.text: Wrong details can mislead and upset
To save time in the conversation

mcq.explanation: Guessing at causes or details can turn out wrong, which misleads the patient and causes more upset; say what you know.

mcq.q: Should you offer a second opinion after an error?
mcq.explanation: Offering a second opinion, where appropriate, helps restore the patient's confidence in their care.

mcq.q: Which tone suits an apology?
mcq.explanation: A calm, sincere and respectful tone shows you take what happened seriously.

mcq.q: An apology conversation should take place

options.text: at the front desk, as they leave
in a busy corridor between clinics

mcq.explanation: Apologies need a private, unhurried place so the patient can talk freely and ask questions.

mcq.q: What should a written apology include?

options.text: What happened, the apology, what's next and contacts
The word 'sorry' and nothing more than that
An explanation of which colleague was to blame
Nothing in writing: say it all in person

mcq.explanation: A written apology should explain what happened, say sorry, set out what's next and give contact details.

mcq.q: Why mention what will change to prevent it happening again?

options.text: It shows lessons have been learned
It isn't needed after an apology
To avoid being blamed for it

mcq.explanation: Explaining what will change shows the patient that lessons have been learned and it's less likely to happen to someone else.

mcq.q: A patient wants to make a formal complaint after an apology. What do you do?

options.text: Explain the procedure and support them

mcq.explanation: Patients have the right to complain even after an apology; explain the procedure and support them through it.

mcq.q: Which cultural factor might affect an apology?

options.text: Language needs and who they want there

mcq.explanation: Language needs, interpreters and who the patient wants present can all affect how an apology should be given.

mcq.q: Should a student apologise alone for a serious error?
mcq.explanation: For a serious error a student should involve their supervisor, who is responsible for the patient's care and can support the conversation.

mcq.q: Which is a sincere-sounding apology?

options.text: 'I'm sorry we didn't refer you sooner. Here's the plan.'
'Sorry if you were upset by what happened.'
'Things like this happen in busy clinics.'
'It's the system's fault, not ours really.'

mcq.explanation: A sincere apology names what went wrong and what happens next. 'Sorry if you were upset' is conditional and shifts the focus to the patient.

mcq.q: An apology is mainly about
mcq.explanation: An apology is about treating the patient with respect and honesty, not about avoiding legal action or saving face.

mcq.q: Why record the apology conversation?

options.text: It's part of the record for any review
To use against the patient later
So the practice can bill for it

mcq.explanation: Recording the apology conversation means there's an accurate account for any later review or investigation.

mcq.q: When should you not delay an apology?

options.text: Almost always: don't wait for blame
Wait for a year to be sure

mcq.explanation: An apology isn't an admission of liability, so it should almost never be delayed while blame is worked out.

mcq.q: Which body language supports an apology?
mcq.explanation: Sitting at the patient's level and making eye contact shows respect and openness; standing over them or crossed arms seem defensive.

mcq.q: How should you respond if the patient blames you unfairly?

options.text: Listen, acknowledge and stick to facts
Argue back to correct what they said
Walk away until they have calmed down
Blame a colleague who was also involved

mcq.explanation: If the patient blames you unfairly, listen and acknowledge their feelings, and stick to the facts rather than arguing or blaming others.

mcq.q: After an apology, follow-up should

options.text: check on how the patient is doing

mcq.explanation: Follow-up checks how the patient is doing and whether they need anything more, showing ongoing care.

mcq.q: A patient is too upset to talk now. What should you do?

options.text: Offer another time and written information
Push on with the conversation now
Never contact them about it again
Close the case as dealt with

mcq.explanation: If the patient can't talk now, offer another time and written information so they can come back to it when ready.

mcq.q: Apologising for an outcome doesn't mean
mcq.explanation: Saying sorry for what happened isn't an admission of legal liability; the law in the UK protects apologies.

mcq.q: Which is NOT part of a good apology?

options.text: Blaming the patient for not noticing

mcq.explanation: Blaming the patient is never part of a good apology; it undermines trust and the purpose of being candid.

mcq.q: What should you avoid saying about colleagues?
mcq.explanation: Avoid unfounded blame or criticism of colleagues; stick to the known facts.

mcq.q: Why is an apology good for clinicians too?
mcq.explanation: Apologising supports trust with patients and helps clinicians learn from what happened.

cases.scenario: A colleague tells you not to say sorry to a patient after a missed referral, 'because it admits liability'.
cases.question: Is that right, and what makes a good apology?
cases.modelAnswer: It is not right. Saying sorry is not in itself an admission of legal liability, and the GOC expects registrants to apologise when things go wrong. A good apology is prompt, sincere and personal; says clearly what happened and what it means for the patient; takes responsibility without blaming others or making excuses; explains what will be done to put it right and to stop it happening again; and gives the patient a named contact and time to ask questions. Record that you apologised and what was said.

topics.askClaude: Role-play an upset patient whose glasses were made wrongly. Let me apologise and explain, then score me on honesty, clarity and empathy.

topics.title: Raising concerns
topics.summary: If you're worried that patients could be put at risk — by a colleague, a system, or a practice — you have a professional duty to raise it. Start with the right person locally, keep records, and know where to go if that doesn't work. Whistleblowers are legally protected.
keyPoints: You must raise concerns about patient safety, even as a student.
Start locally: your supervisor, clinic lead or manager; at university, the clinic or programme lead.
If immediate patient safety is at risk, act straight away.
Write down what you saw, when, and who you told.
If local routes fail or aren't appropriate, escalate (e.g. employer's senior management, NHS Freedom to Speak Up Guardians, the regulator).
The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who raise genuine concerns in the public interest.
Concerns about yourself (health, competence) should also be raised — seeking help is professional.
examTraps: Going straight to social media or the press.
Waiting until you have 'proof' when patients are at risk.
Thinking students don't have this duty.

diagram.description: A ladder of escalation from bottom to top: Supervisor or clinic lead → Practice/clinic manager or programme lead → Organisation's senior management or Freedom to Speak Up Guardian → Regulator (e.g. GOC). Side note: if immediate risk, act now.

goDeeper.heading: A student example
goDeeper.body: You notice a practitioner at a placement repeatedly skipping fundus examination on patients with diabetes. Note what you've seen (dates, no patient-identifiable details outside records). Raise it with your placement supervisor or university placement lead. They're there to help you handle it safely and fairly.

goDeeper.heading: Why speaking up matters
goDeeper.body: Many serious failures in healthcare were noticed by someone who felt unable to speak. A culture where people can raise concerns early — without blame — protects patients and staff. Raising a concern is about safety, not about getting someone into trouble.

flashcards.front: First person to raise a clinic concern with (student)
If patient safety is at immediate risk

options.text: Raise it promptly with your placement supervisor
options.feedback: Yes — start with the local route.
Inappropriate and doesn't fix the problem.

options.text: Say nothing — you're only a student
options.feedback: Students have a duty to raise concerns.

mcq.explanation: Infection-control risks affect patient safety; raise it with the right person promptly and record it.

mcq.q: Must students raise patient safety concerns?
mcq.explanation: Students have the same duty as registrants to raise concerns about patient safety; the GOC student standards require it.

mcq.q: On placement you notice equipment isn't being cleaned between patients. Where should you usually start?

options.text: Social media, to warn other students
The police, as it's a public risk

mcq.explanation: Start locally (supervisor, manager) unless that isn't safe or has already failed. Then escalate, e.g. to the GOC.

options.text: Locally: your supervisor, clinic lead or manager

mcq.q: You see a colleague about to instil the wrong drug into a child's eye. What do you do?

options.text: Stop it at once, then report it
Write it down to report later

options.text: What you saw, when, and who you told
Your opinion of the colleague's personality

mcq.explanation: Write down what you saw, when, and who you told.

mcq.q: An optometrist fears being sacked for reporting unsafe practice. Which law protects workers who raise genuine concerns?
mcq.explanation: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers raising genuine concerns in the public interest.

original.q: Which law protects workers raising genuine concerns?

mcq.q: Who can help in the NHS if local routes fail?

options.text: A Freedom to Speak Up Guardian

mcq.explanation: Freedom to Speak Up Guardians help NHS staff raise concerns when normal local routes haven't worked.

mcq.q: A student notices their own anxiety is affecting their clinical decisions. What should they do?

options.text: Raise it and seek help: that's professional

mcq.explanation: Concerns about your own health or competence should also be raised.

original.q: Concerns about your own health or competence should be

mcq.q: Escalation beyond local routes may go to

options.text: senior managers, a Guardian or the regulator
nobody: local routes are the end

mcq.explanation: If local routes fail, escalate to senior managers, a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian or a regulator such as the GOC.

mcq.q: Why raise concerns early?

options.text: To protect patients before harm happens

mcq.explanation: Raising concerns early means problems are fixed before patients are harmed.

mcq.q: In the NHS, who supports staff to speak up?

options.text: A Freedom to Speak Up Guardian

mcq.explanation: In the NHS, Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support staff to raise concerns and make sure they're acted on.

mcq.q: Do you need proof before raising a concern?

options.text: No: a reasonable belief is enough

mcq.explanation: You only need a reasonable belief that something is wrong. It's for others to investigate and gather proof.

mcq.q: Raising a concern confidentially means

options.text: your name is known but protected

mcq.explanation: Raising a concern confidentially means the person receiving it knows who you are but won't share your name without your agreement.

mcq.q: Should you investigate the concern yourself?

options.text: No: report it and let others investigate
Yes, gather all the evidence first
Always, before anyone else is told

mcq.explanation: Report what you've seen and let the right people investigate; investigating yourself can cause harm or affect the outcome.

mcq.q: Who can a student raise concerns with?
mcq.explanation: Students can raise concerns with their supervisor or their university, which have processes to support them.

mcq.q: A friend asks you not to report their repeated unsafe practice. What should guide you?

options.feedback: Not if patients are at risk.

mcq.explanation: Your duty is to patients first. Loyalty to a friend doesn't override reporting unsafe practice.

original.q: What comes first: patient safety or loyalty to colleagues?

mcq.q: Workers raising genuine concerns are protected from
mcq.explanation: Whistleblowing law protects workers who raise genuine concerns from victimisation, such as being treated unfairly or dismissed.

mcq.q: Which body can you go to if local routes fail?

options.text: The GOC or another prescribed body

mcq.explanation: If local routes fail, you can go to the GOC or another prescribed body and still be protected.

mcq.q: Why keep a record of what you saw?
mcq.explanation: A dated record of what you saw and who you told helps if the concern is investigated later.

mcq.q: A colleague seems impaired by alcohol at work. What do you do?
mcq.explanation: A colleague impaired by alcohol puts patients at risk, so it must be raised promptly with the right person.

mcq.q: The GOC is a 'prescribed person' for whistleblowing, which means

options.text: you can raise concerns with it and stay protected
it employs whistleblowers to inspect practices
it bans concerns from being raised externally

mcq.explanation: As a 'prescribed person', the GOC is a body workers can raise concerns with and still have whistleblowing protection.

mcq.q: Which office supports Freedom to Speak Up Guardians in England?
mcq.explanation: The National Guardian's Office leads and supports the network of Freedom to Speak Up Guardians in England.

mcq.q: Raising a concern anonymously can make it
mcq.explanation: If a concern is anonymous, investigators can't ask follow-up questions, so it's harder to look into.

mcq.q: Going to the media is usually

options.text: a last resort, with stricter conditions
the first step to take when worried
required by the GOC before other routes

mcq.explanation: Going to the media is a last resort with stricter legal conditions for protection; use internal and regulator routes first.

mcq.q: Which concern should be raised?

options.text: A colleague who keeps skipping infection control
A colleague's hairstyle that you don't like
A patient's choice of frame that seems odd

mcq.explanation: Skipping infection control puts patients at real risk, so it's a genuine safety concern to raise.

mcq.q: Bullying in the workplace should be

options.text: tolerated as part of the job
ignored in case it gets worse

mcq.explanation: Bullying should be raised through workplace procedures; it harms staff and, through them, patient care.

mcq.q: Who can support an optometrist raising a concern?
mcq.explanation: Professional bodies such as the AOP and unions can advise and support optometrists raising a concern.

mcq.q: Why should you stick to facts when raising a concern?

options.text: It keeps the concern clear and fair

mcq.explanation: Sticking to facts keeps the concern clear and fair, so it can be investigated properly.

mcq.q: A locum notices unsafe practice at a practice they visit. Should they raise it?

options.text: Yes, locally and beyond if needed
Only after they've left the practice

mcq.explanation: Every registrant has the duty to raise concerns, including locums; they should raise it locally and escalate if needed.

mcq.q: What's the risk of not raising a concern?
mcq.explanation: If a concern isn't raised, the risk stays and patients may be harmed.

mcq.q: Gossip about a colleague is

options.text: not a proper way to raise concerns
the best route to raise concerns

mcq.explanation: Gossip doesn't get a concern to anyone who can act on it, and it's unfair to the person involved.

mcq.q: A concern about a GOC registrant's fitness to practise can be raised by
mcq.explanation: Anyone, including patients, colleagues and employers, can raise a fitness to practise concern about a registrant with the GOC.

mcq.q: Whistleblowing law protects workers from
mcq.explanation: Whistleblowing law protects workers from detriment or dismissal for making genuine protected disclosures.

mcq.q: A protected disclosure should usually be made

options.text: believing it's in the public interest
for some personal gain or benefit
to get revenge on a colleague
anonymously, and in no other way

mcq.explanation: For legal protection, a disclosure should usually be made in the reasonable belief that it's in the public interest.

mcq.q: You raised a concern but nothing happened. What next?
mcq.explanation: If nothing happens, escalate to someone more senior or to an external body such as the GOC.

mcq.q: A student on placement is repeatedly rude to patients. Who should a fellow student tell?
mcq.explanation: Concerns about a student's behaviour on placement go to the supervisor and university.

original.q: Concerns about a student's behaviour on placement should go to

mcq.q: Which is a patient safety concern?
mcq.explanation: Uncalibrated equipment can give wrong readings, such as IOP, leading to missed disease; that's a patient safety issue.

mcq.q: Why reflect after raising a concern?

options.text: To change your account of events
So the clinic can bill for it

mcq.explanation: Reflecting afterwards helps you learn from the experience and look after your own wellbeing.

mcq.q: Should you raise a concern about yourself, e.g. your health affecting work?
mcq.explanation: If your own health might affect your work, you should raise it and get help early, before patients are put at risk.

mcq.q: If a manager is the subject of your concern, you should
mcq.explanation: If the manager is the subject of the concern, go to someone more senior or to another route, to avoid a conflict of interest.

mcq.q: Which is a reason people don't raise concerns?

options.feedback: Yes, which protections aim to reduce.

mcq.explanation: Fear of consequences, such as blame or damage to relationships, is a common reason people stay silent; protections aim to reduce it.

mcq.q: Why should organisations welcome concerns?
mcq.explanation: Organisations that welcome concerns catch problems early, before patients are harmed.

mcq.q: Raising a concern is different from making a complaint because

options.text: it's about risk to others, not you

mcq.explanation: A concern is about a risk to others, such as patients; a complaint is usually about how you yourself have been treated.

mcq.q: If a patient is in immediate danger, you should
mcq.explanation: If a patient is in immediate danger, protect them first, then report what happened.

mcq.q: Which records should you keep about your concern?

options.text: Dates, what you saw and who you told

mcq.explanation: Keep dated notes of what you saw and who you told, sticking to relevant facts.

mcq.q: Patient safety concerns about a pharmacy should go to

options.text: the GOC, as the optical regulator
the DVLA, as it affects safety

mcq.explanation: Raise it first with the pharmacy, and if needed with its regulator, the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC).

mcq.q: The duty to raise concerns overrides
mcq.explanation: Patient safety comes first: the duty to raise concerns overrides loyalty to colleagues.

mcq.q: Students worried about raising a concern can get advice from
mcq.explanation: Students can get advice from their tutor or university support services before or while raising a concern.

mcq.q: What's a 'detriment' in whistleblowing law?
mcq.explanation: A detriment is any unfair treatment, such as demotion, being denied training or bullying, because you made a protected disclosure.

mcq.q: Which outcome shows a concern was handled well?

options.text: The risk was fixed and the reporter supported
The person who raised it was blamed
Nothing changed but it was noted
It was kept secret from everyone

mcq.explanation: A concern is handled well when the risk is dealt with and the person who raised it is supported, not blamed.

cases.scenario: You repeatedly see a colleague leave the tonometer prism unwiped between patients. When you mention it, they say there isn't time.
cases.question: What should you do?
cases.modelAnswer: Patient safety comes first, and you have a professional duty to act. You have raised it informally, so now escalate: report it to your supervisor, manager or the practice's clinical lead, sticking to what you saw and when, and keep your own dated note. If nothing changes, escalate further inside the organisation and then, if patients remain at risk, to the regulator; the GOC's guidance on speaking up sets out the route, and whistleblowing law protects workers who raise genuine concerns. Staying silent is itself a breach of the standards.

topics.title: Equality, diversity and inclusion
topics.summary: Your legal and professional duties not to discriminate, how unconscious bias creeps into care, and the reasonable adjustments that make a practice accessible.
keyPoints: GOC standard 13.2: promote equality, value diversity, be inclusive and don't discriminate on any protected characteristic.
Equality Act 2010, nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

College of Optometrists guidance: don't discriminate against patients (D9) or colleagues (C165). An employer who fails to protect a colleague from racist comments by staff or patients may breach C165.
NHS contracts carry equality obligations, such as the Workforce Race Equality Standard.
Unconscious bias: understand its impact, use logical checks on yourself, and don't become complacent.
Section 20 reasonable adjustments: step-free access, easy-read letters, priority or longer appointments, a quiet waiting space, hearing loops, communication charts for dementia.
examTraps: Listing 'gender' instead of 'sex' and 'gender reassignment' as the Act's protected characteristics.
Using a family member as interpreter without thinking about whether consent is truly informed.
Treating everyone the same and calling it equality: reasonable adjustments mean treating people differently so they get the same access.

goDeeper.heading: Case: a transgender patient
goDeeper.body: A 20-year-old's record says female; he tells you he is transgender and uses he/him, and the receptionist called out his old name. In the room: apologise, use his name and pronouns, and check how he'd like to be recorded. Longer term: update records and systems, train staff, and challenge inappropriate language when you hear it.

goDeeper.heading: Case: language and cultural beliefs
goDeeper.body: A 65-year-old woman new to the UK speaks little English; her son interprets and she is afraid of drops that will 'harm her vision'. Think about professional interpreters, explaining what drops are for (and that they are optional), checking understanding before consent, and whether the son is filtering what she says or hears.

flashcards.back: Age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.

flashcards.front: Which section of the Equality Act covers reasonable adjustments?

flashcards.back: Standard 13.2: promote equality, value diversity and be inclusive.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?

options.feedback: Correct: it isn't one of the nine.

mcq.explanation: The Equality Act 2010 lists nine protected characteristics; social class isn't one of them.

mcq.q: How many protected characteristics does the Equality Act 2010 list?
mcq.explanation: The Equality Act 2010 lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

mcq.q: A practice declines to offer a pregnant optometrist a placement because she's pregnant. Which protected characteristic is involved?
mcq.explanation: Pregnancy and maternity is one of the nine protected characteristics.

original.q: Which is a protected characteristic?

mcq.q: A patient who has transitioned is repeatedly misgendered by staff on purpose. Which protected characteristic is involved?
mcq.explanation: Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010.

original.q: Which is a protected characteristic?

mcq.q: The Public Sector Equality Duty applies to

options.text: public bodies, such as the NHS

mcq.explanation: The Public Sector Equality Duty requires public bodies, including the NHS, to consider equality in their decisions and services.

mcq.q: The NHS Accessible Information Standard requires services to

options.text: communicate with patients in English only
stop using interpreters for any patient
treat every patient's needs the same way

mcq.explanation: The Accessible Information Standard requires NHS and adult social care services to identify and meet patients' communication needs linked to disability or sensory loss.

mcq.q: The duty to make reasonable adjustments is 'anticipatory', meaning

options.text: services should plan for disabled people's needs in advance
adjustments are made only after complaints

mcq.explanation: An anticipatory duty means services must plan ahead for disabled people's needs, rather than wait for someone to ask.

mcq.q: An autistic patient may benefit from

options.text: a quiet room and a clear plan

mcq.explanation: Many autistic people find noise and uncertainty stressful, so a quiet room and a clear plan of what will happen help.

mcq.q: A patient who can't climb stairs needs

options.text: step-free access or a home visit

mcq.explanation: Making a reasonable adjustment, such as step-free access or a home visit, means the patient isn't excluded from care.

mcq.q: Positive action means

options.text: lawful steps to help under-represented groups

mcq.explanation: Positive action is lawful action, such as targeted outreach, to help under-represented or disadvantaged groups; it isn't discrimination against others.

mcq.q: Intersectionality describes
mcq.explanation: Intersectionality describes how different characteristics, such as race, sex and disability, overlap and combine to shape someone's experience.

mcq.q: A patient asks for a practitioner of the same sex for cultural reasons. What should you do?

options.text: Refuse every request of this kind

mcq.explanation: Requests for a practitioner of the same sex for cultural reasons should be met where reasonably possible, as part of respectful care.

mcq.q: Using someone's correct name and pronouns is part of
mcq.explanation: Using someone's correct name and pronouns shows respect and is part of inclusive care.

mcq.q: Discrimination arising from disability means

options.text: unfair treatment because of something linked to it
treating everyone in exactly the same way

mcq.explanation: Discrimination arising from disability is treating someone unfavourably because of something linked to their disability, such as needing more time.

mcq.q: Cultural competence in healthcare means
mcq.explanation: Cultural competence means understanding and respecting patients' different backgrounds and adapting care accordingly.

mcq.q: Allyship means

options.text: taking legal action and nothing else

mcq.explanation: Allyship means actively supporting people who face discrimination, for example by challenging it when you see it.

mcq.q: A colleague mimics a patient's accent. What should you do?

options.text: Challenge it and report if needed
Laugh along with it to keep the peace
Join in so that you fit in with the team
Ignore it this time and see if it recurs

mcq.explanation: Mocking a patient's accent is discriminatory, so challenge it and report it if needed; laughing along condones it.

mcq.q: Which group may face barriers to eye care?
mcq.explanation: People with learning disabilities often face barriers to eye care, such as communication and access, and have higher rates of eye problems.

mcq.q: Why monitor equality data in services?

options.text: To find and fix unequal access

mcq.explanation: Monitoring equality data shows whether some groups have poorer access or outcomes, so services can act on it.

mcq.q: Which adjustment helps a patient with dyslexia?

options.text: Clear spoken and accessible written information
Dense small print to read at home
Rushing so they aren't kept waiting

mcq.explanation: Clear spoken explanations and accessible written information, such as larger, clearer fonts, help patients with dyslexia.

mcq.q: Age discrimination would be

options.text: refusing a test simply because someone is old
giving a free NHS test to over-60s

mcq.explanation: Refusing a service only because of someone's age is direct age discrimination; adjusting care for age-related needs is fine.

mcq.q: Which is an inclusive form question about sex and gender?

options.text: One that lets people describe themselves
One that forces a single fixed answer
None: never ask about sex or gender
One with a joke option to lighten it

mcq.explanation: Letting people describe themselves is more inclusive than forcing a fixed answer, while still getting the information needed for records.

mcq.q: Unconscious bias can affect
mcq.explanation: Unconscious bias can shape clinical decisions and how we communicate with patients, without us noticing.

mcq.q: Which is a reasonable adjustment for a wheelchair user at the slit lamp?

options.text: Adjustable equipment or a movable table
Asking them to stand for the test
Nothing: they must manage as they are

mcq.explanation: Adjustable equipment or a movable table lets a wheelchair user be examined at the slit lamp without standing or missing the test.

mcq.q: Racial harassment at work should be

options.text: tolerated as part of the job
joked about to lighten the mood

mcq.explanation: Racial harassment must be reported and dealt with; ignoring it lets it continue and breaches the employer's duties.

mcq.q: Why is equality, diversity and inclusion part of professional standards?

options.text: It helps the practice with billing

mcq.explanation: Professional standards require everyone to be treated fairly and without discrimination.

mcq.q: What does 'inclusion' add beyond diversity?

options.text: People feel valued and can take part

mcq.explanation: Diversity is about having different people present; inclusion means they feel valued and are able to take part fully.

mcq.q: A patient refuses to be seen by a practitioner because of their race. What should happen?

options.text: Follow policy and support the staff member
Always agree, as the patient chooses
Ignore the request and carry on
Argue with the patient in public

mcq.explanation: A request based on race shouldn't simply be granted: follow the practice's policy and support the staff member.

mcq.q: Which is an example of indirect discrimination?

options.text: Requiring all patients to book online only
Refusing someone because of their religion

mcq.explanation: Online-only booking applies to everyone but disadvantages groups such as older or disabled people with less internet access: indirect discrimination.

mcq.q: Which law requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people?
mcq.explanation: The Equality Act 2010 places a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people.

mcq.q: Why use plain English in patient materials?
mcq.explanation: Plain English is easier for everyone to understand, including people with lower literacy or who don't speak English as a first language.

mcq.q: How many protected characteristics are in the Equality Act 2010?
mcq.explanation: The nine are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

mcq.q: Which is a reasonable adjustment?
mcq.explanation: A longer appointment helps a disabled patient access care on equal terms, so it's a reasonable adjustment.

mcq.q: What should you do if a colleague makes a discriminatory comment?
mcq.explanation: Discriminatory comments should be challenged and raised; ignoring them lets them continue.

mcq.q: A wheelchair user can't reach your consulting room. Under which section of the Equality Act must you consider changes such as step-free access?
mcq.explanation: Section 20 covers reasonable adjustments such as step-free access and easy-read letters.

original.q: Which section of the Equality Act covers reasonable adjustments?

mcq.q: How can you tackle unconscious bias?

options.text: Know its impact, check yourself and stay alert
Assume you have none to deal with
Ignore it, as it's unconscious anyway

mcq.explanation: Tackling unconscious bias means knowing how it can affect care, checking your own decisions and staying alert to it.

mcq.q: Which GOC standard covers equality?
mcq.explanation: GOC standard 13 covers not discriminating; 13.2 is about making reasonable adjustments and treating patients fairly.

mcq.q: A patient tells you they use he/him pronouns but the record says female. What do you do?

options.text: Use his name and pronouns, and update the record
Ask for proof before changing anything

mcq.explanation: Use the name and pronouns the patient tells you, and update the record so it's accurate.

mcq.q: Why might using a family member as an interpreter be a problem?
mcq.explanation: A family member may filter, soften or leave out what's said, and may affect confidentiality, so a professional interpreter is safer.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a protected characteristic?
mcq.explanation: Social class isn't one of the nine protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010.

mcq.q: Treating someone worse because of a protected characteristic is
mcq.explanation: Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic is direct discrimination.

mcq.q: A rule that applies to everyone but disadvantages a group is
mcq.explanation: A rule applied to everyone that puts a particular group at a disadvantage is indirect discrimination, unless it can be justified.

mcq.q: Treating someone badly because they made a complaint is
mcq.explanation: Treating someone badly because they made or supported a complaint of discrimination is victimisation.

mcq.q: Equity means
mcq.explanation: Equity means giving people what they need for a fair outcome, which may differ from person to person.

mcq.q: Which adjustment helps a patient with low vision?
mcq.explanation: Large-print information lets a patient with low vision read it independently.

mcq.q: Which helps hearing-aid users?
mcq.explanation: A hearing loop sends sound directly to hearing aids set to the T setting, cutting out background noise.

mcq.q: What are microaggressions?

options.text: Small remarks that demean a group

mcq.explanation: Microaggressions are small, often unintended, remarks or actions that demean a person or group.

mcq.q: How can bias in clinic be reduced?
mcq.explanation: Awareness, training and structured processes, such as checklists, reduce the effect of bias on decisions.

mcq.q: Unwanted conduct that violates dignity is
mcq.explanation: Unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates someone's dignity or creates a hostile environment is harassment.

mcq.q: Which law lists the nine protected characteristics?
mcq.explanation: The Equality Act 2010 sets out the protected characteristics.

original.q: Which law sets out protected characteristics?

cases.scenario: A profoundly deaf patient who uses British Sign Language books an eye examination. The practice suggests they bring their 12-year-old child to interpret.
cases.question: What is wrong with that and what should happen instead?
cases.modelAnswer: Relying on a child to interpret is inappropriate: it compromises accuracy, confidentiality and valid consent, and puts an unfair burden on the child. Under the Equality Act 2010 the practice must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Offer a qualified BSL interpreter (in person or by video), allow a longer appointment, face the patient in good light, use written and visual explanations, and ask the patient what works best for them. Record their communication needs so the adjustment is in place for every visit.
